questions.stem:
The Venn diagram, where $p$ and $q$ are probabilities, shows the three events $A$, $B$ and $C$ and their associated probabilities.

$\mathrm{P}(A \cap B' \cap C') = 0.13\qquad \mathrm{P}(A \cap B \cap C') = 0.25\qquad \mathrm{P}(A' \cap B \cap C') = 0.05\qquad \mathrm{P}(A' \cap B \cap C) = 0.3\qquad \mathrm{P}(A' \cap B' \cap C) = p\qquad \mathrm{P}(A' \cap B' \cap C') = q$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find $\mathrm{P}(A)$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $[0.13+0.25=]$ $0.38$ B1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for 0.38 (or exact equivalent). If answers are given on Venn Diagram and in the script then the script takes precedence.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The events $B$ and $C$ are independent.
(b) Find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Independence implies:
e.g. $\left[\mathrm{P}(B \cap C) = \mathrm{P}(B) \times \mathrm{P}(C) \Rightarrow\right] 0.3 = (0.3+0.05+0.25) \times (0.3+p)$ M1
So $p=0.2$ A1
[Sum of probabilities = 1 gives] $q=0.07$ B1ft
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for a correct equation in p or P(C) only. May be implied by an answer of $p = 0.2$ provided this does not come from incorrect working. Condone missing brackets if they get 0.2. Other rules for independence will give simple rearrangements of this equation.
- Beware: If $p = 0.2$ comes from incorrect working, we've seen $p=\frac{0.6}{0.3}=0.2$, score M0A0
- A1 for $p = 0.2$ (or exact equivalent). B1ft for $q = 0.07$ (or exact equivalent) ft their p i.e. $q = 0.27 - \text{"0.2"}$ where $0 \leqslant p \leqslant 0.27$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find $\mathrm{P}(A \mid B')$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $\left[\mathrm{P}(A \mid B') = \right] \dfrac{\mathrm{P}(A \cap B')}{\mathrm{P}(B')}$ or $\dfrac{0.13}{(1-0.6)}$ or $\dfrac{0.13}{0.13+"0.2"+"0.07"}$ M1
$=\dfrac{13}{40}$ or $0.325$ A1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for a correct ratio of probability expressions or a correct ratio of probabilities ft their values of p and q (provided both probabilities) or letters p and q. A1 for 0.325 or exact equivalent. Correct answer only will score 2/2. NB on epen this is labelled M1 but treat it as A1

questions.stem:
A machine fills packets with sweets and $\dfrac{1}{7}$ of the packets also contain a prize.
The packets of sweets are placed in boxes before being delivered to shops.
There are 40 packets of sweets in each box.
The random variable $T$ represents the number of packets of sweets that contain a prize
in each box.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) State a condition needed for $T$ to be modelled by $\mathrm{B}(40, \frac{1}{7})$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) Comment in context about either independence or random packing e.g.
“prizes must be placed in packets at random/independently of each other”
or about constant probability e.g.
“the probability of a packet containing a prize is constant/the same/fixed” B1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 May use idea of independent events: a suitable reason, in context, covering idea of random packing or packets filled independently. Should mention key words/ideas of: prizes in packets or packets in boxes. May use idea of constant probability. Must see key words underlined in scheme. Idea of probability with "independence" or "not affected by other packets" is B0. B0 for: Idea of only 2 cases. E.g. Packet contains a prize or not or Idea of a fixed number of trials. E.g. Need a fixed number of packets in each box

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A box is selected at random.
(b) Using $T \sim \mathrm{B}(40, \frac{1}{7})$ find
(i) the probability that the box has exactly 6 packets containing a prize,
(ii) the probability that the box has fewer than 3 packets containing a prize.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b)(i) $[\mathrm{P}(T=6)=]$ $0.17273\ldots$ awrt $0.173$ B1
(ii) $[\mathrm{P}(T<3)=\mathrm{P}(T \leqslant 2)=]$ $0.061587\ldots$ awrt $0.0616$ B1

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Kamil’s sweet shop buys 5 boxes of these sweets.
(c) Find the probability that exactly 2 of these 5 boxes have fewer than 3 packets
containing a prize.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $[K = $ no. of boxes with fewer than 3 packets containing a prize$]$
$K \sim \mathrm{B}(5, \text{"}0.0616\text{"})$ M1
$\mathrm{P}(K=2) = 0.031344\ldots$ in the range $[0.0313 \sim 0.0314]$ A1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for sight of B(5, "0.0616") or ${}^5C_2(\text{"0.0616"})^2(1-\text{"0.0616"})^3$ ft their answer to (b)(ii). A1 for an answer in the range [0.0313 to 0.0314] Use of 0.0616 gives 0.031356..ans only 2/2

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Kamil claims that the proportion of packets containing a prize is less than $\dfrac{1}{7}$
A random sample of 110 packets is taken and 9 packets contain a prize.
(d) Use a suitable test to assess Kamil’s claim.
You should
$\bullet$ state your hypotheses clearly
$\bullet$ use a 5% level of significance
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $\mathrm{H_0}: p = \frac{1}{7}$ $\mathrm{H_1}: p < \frac{1}{7}$ B1
$[X = $ no of packets containing a prize$]$ $X \sim \mathrm{B}(110, \frac{1}{7})$ M1
$[\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 9)=]$ $0.038292\ldots$ A1
[Significant result or reject $\mathrm{H_0}$]
e.g. there is evidence to support Kamil’s claim A1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for both hypotheses correct in terms of p or $\pi$. M1 for selecting an appropriate model, may be implied by 1st A1 or $\mathrm{P}(X=9) = 0.0199(2\ldots)$. 1st A1 for 0.038 or better or allow 0.04 with sight of $\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 9)$
- ALT Critical Region. Allow CR of $X \leqslant 9$ (or $X<10$) provided a supporting probability is seen e.g. A1 for correct CR plus $\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 10) = 0.0718\ldots$ (accept 2sf or 1sf if prob statement seen)
- 2nd A1 (dep on 1st A1 but indep of hyp's) for a suitable conclusion in context that suggests support for (Kamil's) claim or states that there is evidence that proportion/probability/chance of packets containing a prize is less than $\frac{1}{7}$. Do not award 2nd A1 for contradictory statements e.g. "not significant" so "supports claim"
- Normal: Sight of $\mathrm{N}\left(\frac{110}{7}, \frac{660}{49}\right)$ or awrt 13.5 or probability of 0.045(20..) or 0.033(66..) scores M1

questions.stem:
Ben is studying the Daily Total Rainfall, $x\,\mathrm{mm}$, in Leeming for 1987
He used all the data from the large data set and summarised the information in the
following table.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 0 & 0.1\text{--}0.5 & 0.6\text{--}1.0 & 1.1\text{--}1.9 & 2.0\text{--}4.0 & 4.1\text{--}6.9 & 7.0\text{--}12.0 & 12.1\text{--}20.9 & 21.0\text{--}32.0 & \mathrm{tr}\\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 55 & 18 & 18 & 21 & 17 & 9 & 9 & 6 & 2 & 29\\ \hline\end{array}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Explain how the data will need to be cleaned before Ben can start to calculate
statistics such as the mean and standard deviation.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) Need to replace tr with a numerical value M1
Value of tr is between 0 and 0.05 suggest using e.g $0.025$, $0$ or value $\leqslant 0.05$ A1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for recognising that tr must be replaced (oe) with a numerical value. The following examples would score M0: The tr values are worth 0 so ignore (not replacing) or must remove outliers or fill gaps in table or make widths the same or need to find mid-points. A1 for using a suitable value: e.g. 0.025 (or allow 0) i.e. any value in [0, 0.05] (these give $\sum x = 390$ (3sf), use of 0.05 gives 390.8, use of 0 gives 389.3 allow in (b)(i))

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Using all 184 of these values, Ben estimates $\sum x = 390$ and $\sum x^2 = 4336$

(b) Calculate estimates for
(i) the mean Daily Total Rainfall,
(ii) the standard deviation of the Daily Total Rainfall.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b)(i) $\left[\bar{x} = \dfrac{389.3 \sim 390.8}{184}\right] = 2.119\ldots$ awrt $2.12$ allow $\dfrac{195}{92}$ or $2\frac{11}{92}$ B1
(ii) $[\sigma=]\sqrt{\dfrac{(\text{awrt}4336)}{184} - "\bar{x}"^2}$ or allow $\left[\sigma^2=\right]\dfrac{(\text{awrt}4336)}{184} - "\bar{x}"^2$ or awrt $19.1$ M1
$=4.367\ldots$ awrt $4.37$ A1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (b)(i) B1 for awrt 2.12 or allow simplified fraction or mixed number. B0 for $\frac{390}{184}$
- (ii) M1 for a correct expression for standard deviation or variance. Allow $\sum x^2 =$ awrt 4336. Ignore their label $\sigma$ or $\sigma^2$. Can ft their mean. A1 for awrt 4.37 [Use of s gives 4.3791… so for correct use seen allow awrt 4.38]
- SC Using n = 155 Allow M1 for expression $[\sigma=]\sqrt{\frac{(\text{awrt})4336}{155} - \text{"}\bar{x}^2\text{"}} = \sqrt{21.64\ldots}$ or 4.65…

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Ben suggests using the statistic calculated in part (b)(i) to estimate the annual mean
Daily Total Rainfall in Leeming for 1987
(c) Using your knowledge of the large data set,
(i) give a reason why these data would not be suitable,
(ii) state, giving a reason, how you would expect the estimate in part (b)(i) to differ
from the actual annual mean Daily Total Rainfall in Leeming for 1987
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(i) Only covers May–Oct (so not a suitable sample) B1
(ii) e.g. Winter months are missing when we’d expect more rain
so expect estimate in (b)(i) to be an underestimate (oe) B1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Part (c) can effectively be marked together. (c)(i) B1 for a comment mentioning that data is just from May~Oct (so not representative of the whole year). Just saying "only 184 days so not representative" is B0, must mention May ~ Oct
- (ii) B1 for comment that missing/winter months expected to have more rain (oe) and "underestimate"(oe). We are looking for all 3 of these ideas here: 1. A statement or implication that missing data is from winter or different months. 2. A suggestion about the rainfall in these months (probably more rain). 3. A statement about the impact on the estimate in (b)(i) equivalent to saying it would be an underestimate or the (actual) mean will be higher.
- SC If you see "Leeming or N or NE has less rain in winter months" – please send to review

questions.stem:
A study was made of adult men from region $A$ of a country.
It was found that their heights were normally distributed with a mean of $175.4\,\mathrm{cm}$ and
standard deviation $6.8\,\mathrm{cm}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the proportion of these men that are taller than $180\,\mathrm{cm}$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) $[$Let $N=$ height from region $A$; $\mathrm{P}(N>180)=]$ $0.24937\ldots$ awrt $0.249$ B1

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A student claimed that the mean height of adult men from region $B$ of this country was
different from the mean height of adult men from region $A$.
A random sample of 52 adult men from region $B$ had a mean height of $177.2\,\mathrm{cm}$
The student assumed that the standard deviation of heights of adult men was $6.8\,\mathrm{cm}$ both
for region $A$ and region $B$.
(b) Use a suitable test to assess the student’s claim.
You should
$\bullet$ state your hypotheses clearly
$\bullet$ use a 5% level of significance
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\mathrm{H_0}: \mu = 175.4$ $\mathrm{H_1}: \mu \neq 175.4$ B1
$[S = $ height from region $B]$ $\bar{S} \sim \mathrm{N}\left(175.4, \dfrac{6.8^2}{52}\right)$ Allow $\sigma^2 = $ awrt $0.889$ M1
$[\mathrm{P}(\bar{S}>177.2)]=0.02814\ldots$ A1
$[0.028\ldots > 0.025$, Not sig, do not reject $\mathrm{H_0}]$
Insufficient evidence to support student’s claim A1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for both hypotheses correct in terms of $\mu$ (See below for one-tail test). M1 for selecting the correct model, may be implied by standardisation using correct values or may be implied by a correct value in 1st A1 e.g.(Prob =) 0.028 or awrt 0.972, (Z =) 1.9(08..) (CV=) 177.25. Condone use of S (or any other letter) instead of $\bar{S}$. Condone use of $\bar{S} \sim \mathrm{N}\left(177.2, \frac{6.8^2}{52}\right)$ but this will lose 2nd A mark
- 1st A1 for probability of awrt 0.028 (allow 0.03 if $\mathrm{P}(\bar{S} > 177.2)$ is seen). Condone 1 – 0.02814 … = 0.9718…(awrt 0..972) only if clearly compared with 0.975
- ALT Allow Z = 1.9(088…) and comparison with 1.96 (or better: calc gives 1.95996…) or CR of $[\bar{S}]$… 177.248…(awrt 177.25) Allow $[\bar{S}]>$177.248…(awrt 177.25) Implied by diagram or correct interpretation of inequality with their CV (Ignore any attempt at a lower CR for $\bar{S}$)
- 2nd A1 (dep on 1st A1 and use of correct model. Use of N(177.2, …) scores A0) for a conclusion using context: e.g. does not support student's claim or e.g. insufficient evidence of a difference in heights. Do not allow 2nd A mark for contradictory statements e.g. "significant" so "no support for claim"
- NB One-tail test [Max of 3/5 for (b) and (c)] In (b) B0 (hypotheses) M1(model as above) 1st A1[for probability or Z compared with 1.6449 or CR $[\bar{S}]$… or > 176.95… (awrt 177)] 2nd A1 for conclusion in context that supports claim or "heights of men from B is different from/greater than from A" In (c) B0

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find the $p$-value for the test in part (b)
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $[p\text{-value} = 2 \times 0.02814\ldots =]$ $0.05628\ldots$
in range $0.056 \sim 0.06$ or $5.6(\%) \sim 6(\%)$ B1ft
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1ft for answer in range 0.056~0.06 or 5.6%~6% (Ranges are inclusive, condone missing %) (can ft their probability, provided < 0.5, from part (b) but not 0.025 leading to 5%)

questions.stem:
Tisam is playing a game.
She uses a ball, a cup and a spinner.

The random variable $X$ represents the number the spinner lands on when it is spun.
The probability distribution of $X$ is given in the following table

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 20 & 50 & 80 & 100\\ \hline \mathrm{P}(X=x) & a & b & c & d\\ \hline\end{array}$

where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are probabilities.
To play the game
$\bullet$ the spinner is spun to obtain a value of $x$
$\bullet$ Tisam then stands $x\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the cup and tries to throw the ball into the cup
The event $S$ represents the event that Tisam successfully throws the ball into the cup.
To model this game Tisam assumes that
$\bullet$ $\mathrm{P}(S \mid \{X=x\}) = \dfrac{k}{x}$ where $k$ is a constant
$\bullet$ $\mathrm{P}(S \cap \{X=x\})$ should be the same whatever value of $x$ is obtained from the spinner

Using Tisam’s model,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) show that $c = \dfrac{8}{5}b$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\mathrm{P}(S \cap \{X=50\}) = \mathrm{P}(S \cap \{X=80\})[=\text{a constant}, V] \Rightarrow b \times \dfrac{k}{50} = c \times \dfrac{k}{80}$ M1
May see: $\dfrac{k}{50} = \dfrac{V}{b}$ and $\dfrac{k}{80} = \dfrac{V}{c}$ (condone any letter for $V$ even $S$)
So $c = \dfrac{8}{5}b$ * A1cso*
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for use of $\mathrm{P}(S \mid X=x) \times \mathrm{P}(X=x)$ for x = 50 and x = 80 (Must see k or their V) Any expression or equation MUST be based on the probability statements in qu. A1cso for rearranging to required result, no incorrect work seen, condone poor notation
- NB Use of values e.g. $b = \frac{50}{20+50+80+100}$ to prove (a) is M0A0 but scores 2nd M1A1 in (b)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) find the probability distribution of $X$
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $d=2b$ or $a=\dfrac{2}{5}b$ or $c=4a$ or $d=5a$ or $d=\dfrac{5}{4}c$ M1
A1
$\dfrac{2}{5}b + b + \dfrac{8}{5}b + 2b = 1$ M1
$\Rightarrow 5b=1$ so $b=\dfrac{1}{5}$ (o.e.) A1
$a=\dfrac{2}{25}$ $b=\dfrac{1}{5}$ $c=\dfrac{8}{25}$ $d=\dfrac{2}{5}$ A1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Marks for (b) may be awarded for work seen in (a). 1st M1 for at least one other relationship (either probability the subject) from the list. 1st A1 for a second different relationship (either probability the subject) from the list. or Allow for: $\frac{ak}{20}=\frac{bk}{50}=\frac{ck}{80}=\frac{dk}{100}$ for 1st M1 1st A1
- 2nd M1 for using or stating sum of prob's = 1 May be implied by one correct probability. 2nd A1 for one correct probability e.g. b = $\frac{1}{5}$ or exact equivalent such as 0.2. 3rd A1 for all correct probabilities. Allow exact equivalents e.g. c = 0.32. Sight of correct distribution or list of probs with no obvious incorrect working is 5/5

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Nav tries, a large number of times, to throw the ball into the cup from a distance
of 100 cm.
He successfully gets the ball in the cup 30% of the time.
(c) State, giving a reason, why Tisam’s model of this game is not suitable to describe
Nav playing the game for all values of $X$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $[$Experiment suggests for Nav$]$ $\mathrm{P}(S \mid \{X=100\}) = 0.3 \Rightarrow k=30$
or $0.3 = \dfrac{V}{0.4} \Rightarrow V=0.12$
So model won’t work since
$\mathrm{P}(S \mid X=20) = \dfrac{30}{20}$ or $\dfrac{0.12}{0.08}$ and so would be greater than 1 B1
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for deducing k = 30 and giving a suitable example to show model breaks down
